# Safety by limits, not by approval: testing an AI system that has no approval queue

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that the way to keep AI safe is to have a person approve every step. This paper argues otherwise: approval of every step does not scale and is not the same as safety. Limits on what matters, checks that can fail, live verification and automatic revert can be measured, and a person stays the gate only for acts that cannot be undone.

We test the alternative to approval on every step: declared limits on what matters, checks that can fail, live verification, automatic revert and one narrow stop for acts that are both irreversible and identity-bound. Each property is measured; the ones that fall short are open work.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 6 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

A common belief holds that the way to keep an AI system safe is to have a person approve each step. Ultrastable has no approval queue. It bounds its essential variables, verifies every deploy live, reverts what fails, and pauses only for acts that are both irreversible and bound to the owner's identity. [2]

This matters now because the usual answer, AI is safe only if a person approves every step, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. Everything that matters has limits. Belief: without a person watching, nothing stops a system drifting. Test: share of declared essential variables that have limits. [2]
2. Unreviewed changes are not reverted more. Belief: changes merged without human review get undone. Test: reverts on main per merged pull request. [2]
3. What ships is proven live. Belief: an unapproved deploy could be anything. Test: share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit. [2]
4. The system corrects itself when a limit is crossed. Belief: only a person can correct a system that goes out of bounds. Test: share of second-order steps that brought a variable back inside its limits and were kept. [2]
5. Little work is thrown away. Belief: without approval, a system produces work that has to be discarded. Test: share of closed pull requests closed without merging. [2]
6. One halt stops everything. Belief: an autonomous system cannot be stopped. Test: every registered loop has a server-side owner and closing probe, so one switch reaches each of them. [2]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [1]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [2]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. Everything that matters has limits: an essential variable with no limits fails the check (ASHBY-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
2. Unreviewed changes are not reverted more: only a change whose checks pass merges (AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1, `seed/worker/src/sweeper.js`); a red main is repaired by bisection and the smallest revert (RUNWAY-1, `foundation/redmain.py`)
3. What ships is proven live: a deploy counts only after the live read-back matches its commit (HANDOFF-1, `deploy/deploy-workers.mjs`)
4. The system corrects itself when a limit is crossed: the second loop keeps changing a parameter until the variable holds, and reverts a step that did not help (ASHBY-SEARCH-1, `foundation/ultrastability.py`)
5. Little work is thrown away: a failing detector files its own item with root-cause suspects, so failed work becomes a fix (FAILURE-RESOLVE-1, `foundation/failure_audit.py`)
6. One halt stops everything: one worker variable or committed file stops every cron, webhook and workflow job (HALT-1, `seed/worker/src/budget.js`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. Everything that matters has limits. Put in place: an essential variable with no limits fails the check. Check it with one number, share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json), and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
2. Unreviewed changes are not reverted more. Put in place: only a change whose checks pass merges. Check it with one number, commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window, and set a limit for it (<= 0.05 is the limit we use).
3. What ships is proven live. Put in place: a deploy counts only after the live read-back matches its commit. Check it with one number, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).
4. The system corrects itself when a limit is crossed. Put in place: the second loop keeps changing a parameter until the variable holds, and reverts a step that did not help. Check it with one number, share of second-order steps that brought the variable back inside its limits and were kept, and set a limit for it (>= 0.25 is the limit we use).
5. Little work is thrown away. Put in place: a failing detector files its own item with root-cause suspects, so failed work becomes a fix. Check it with one number, share of closed pull requests closed without merging, and set a limit for it (<= 0.2 is the limit we use).
6. One halt stops everything. Put in place: one worker variable or committed file stops every cron, webhook and workflow job. Check it with one number, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 4 of 6 of these checks pass today. Share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json) reads 1.0 (n = 18; source: doctrine/ultrastability.json). Commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window reads 0.0 (n = 359; source: git log of main, subjects starting with Revert). Share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit reads 0.999 (n = 875; source: ops/deploys.jsonl (same window)). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Scale. One organization: 500 closed pull requests (359 merged) over 7.87 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 87% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Own R&D question set, regenerated from this system's records, version 2026-11-21; its findings may change in later versions.
